title: Crossword Puzzle
directAnswer: You are given a 10×10 grid where `+` is a blocked cell and `-` is a blank to fill, plus a `;`-separated list of words. Find the maximal horizontal and vertical runs of `-` of length ≥ 2 (the 'slots'), then backtrack: assign an unused word to the first unfilled slot only if its length matches and every overlapping letter is consistent (cell is blank or already holds that letter), recurse, and undo on failure. Because the word count is tiny (≤ 10) and slots are few, the search is small in practice; the worst case is O(W! · L) where W is the number of words and L the slot length.

remember.pattern: Slot enumeration + backtracking with intersection consistency (place → recurse → un-place)
rules: Build **slots** first: scan each row and column for maximal runs of `-` with length **≥ 2** — single blanks are never slots.
A word fits a slot only if **lengths match** AND every cell is either blank (`-`) or already equals the word's letter at that position (intersection consistency).
On backtrack restore **exactly** what each cell held before — save a per-cell backup, not a blanket reset to `-`, because crossing words may have written letters first.
Track **used words** so the same word isn't placed twice.
Place words into **slots**, not arbitrary positions — a brute placement that ignores `+` boundaries will overrun a blocked cell.
whenToUse: Fill a fixed grid from a finite word list with crossing constraints
Constraint-satisfaction where each placement restricts later placements
Small search space (few slots / few words) so exponential search is acceptable
Any 'fit pieces into cells respecting overlaps' puzzle (Sudoku, word-fill, KenKen)
antiSignals: Huge word list / large grid → naive backtracking explodes; need constraint propagation or DLX
Words can be reused unlimited times → the used-set bookkeeping changes
No crossing constraints (independent placements) → it's just matching lengths, no search
You only need to check if a single word fits → a simple scan, not backtracking
remember.takeaway: Crossword Puzzle is constraint-satisfaction backtracking on a grid: enumerate the empty slots, then choose → check overlaps → recurse → undo. The discipline that makes it correct is saving each cell's prior contents so a failed branch restores crossings rather than wiping them to blank.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model the grid as a set of slots (maximal blank runs) and run consistent backtracking with proper undo, correctly handling the intersections where two words share a cell.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Restoring backtracked cells to `-` instead of their previous letter (erasing an already-placed crossing word), or placing words at arbitrary offsets without respecting `+` boundaries so a word overruns a blocked cell.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Separate slot-enumeration from search, state that the fit check must allow a cell that already holds the matching letter (the crossing), and note that the small word count keeps the factorial search cheap in practice.

problemStatement:
You are given a **10×10** crossword grid as 10 strings of length 10. A `+` denotes a blocked cell; a `-` denotes a blank to be filled. You are also given a single string of words separated by `;` (e.g. `"LONDON;DELHI;ICELAND;ANKARA"`).

Fill every blank so that each word from the list is placed exactly once, either left-to-right (horizontal) or top-to-bottom (vertical), occupying a maximal run of blanks. Where words cross, the shared cell must agree.

Return the solved grid as 10 strings. A unique solution is guaranteed.
constraints: The number of words equals the number of slots (each word used exactly once)
Every slot is a maximal run of blanks of length ≥ 2
A unique solution is guaranteed to exist
understanding: Think of the grid as a collection of 'slots' — the maximal horizontal and vertical runs of `-`. Each word must occupy exactly one slot of equal length, and wherever a horizontal and vertical slot cross, the letter placed there is shared. The task is to assign words to slots so all crossings agree. With at most a handful of slots and words, a clean choose/check/undo backtracking search finds the unique arrangement.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is every word used exactly once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the number of words equals the number of slots, so each word maps to exactly one slot. Track used words to avoid double placement.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can words be placed diagonally or reversed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Only left-to-right (horizontal) or top-to-bottom (vertical), in the natural reading direction.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What defines a slot's boundaries?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A slot is a maximal run of `-` of length ≥ 2. A `+` or the grid edge terminates it. Single isolated blanks are not slots.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the solution unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the problem guarantees a unique fill, so the first complete assignment the backtracking finds is the answer.

approaches.name: Brute Cell Placement — Place a Word at Any Fitting Position
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the naive first idea, then point out the boundary and overlap pitfalls that motivate slot enumeration.
hints: For the first remaining word, scan every cell and both orientations, and try to drop the word there.

A placement is valid only if the word stays in bounds, every covered cell is `-` or matches the letter, AND the cells just before the start and just after the end are `+` or the edge (so you land on a real slot, not the middle of one).
Recurse on the rest of the words; undo carefully on failure. The boundary check is what stops a word from overrunning a blocked cell.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of W words you may try up to R·C starting cells × 2 orientations, each costing O(L) to validate, and the recursion multiplies these across words — roughly O(W! · R · C · L). The grid copy is O(R·C).
approaches.explanation:
The most direct translation of the problem: take the next word and try to place it *somewhere*. For each grid cell and each of the two orientations, check whether the word fits.

**What 'fits' must mean.** It is not enough that the covered cells are blank or matching — you must also verify the **boundaries**. A horizontal word starting at `(r, c)` is only valid if `c == 0` or `grid[r][c-1] == '+'`, and `c + len == C` or `grid[r][c + len] == '+'`. Without these guards the word can start in the middle of a longer blank run or spill past a `+`, producing a grid that looks filled but violates the slot structure.

**Why it is awkward.** The boundary bookkeeping is exactly the information a slot already encodes. By re-deriving 'is this a real slot?' at every cell for every word, you do the same work repeatedly and invite off-by-one bugs at the edges. It also wastes effort trying thousands of positions that aren't slots at all.

**Why we don't ship it.** It works, but the slot-based version below precomputes the legal positions once, shrinks the branching factor to 'which word goes in this slot', and makes the undo logic trivial. Mention this approach to show you considered the brute force, then refine it.
approaches.insight: The brute version keeps rediscovering where the slots are. Computing slots once turns an O(R·C) position search per word into an O(1) 'next slot' lookup — the same speedup you get by indexing instead of scanning.

diagrams.caption: Without the left/right wall check, a word can start mid-run or overrun a '+'.

pitfalls: Forgetting the before/after boundary check — a word fills the middle of a longer blank run.
Restoring cells to `-` on undo instead of the saved prior contents — erases crossing words.
Re-checking the same non-slot positions for every word — slow and bug-prone.

approaches.name: Slot Enumeration + Backtracking (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean answer. Phrase it as 'precompute the slots, then assign words to slots with overlap-consistent backtracking'.
hints: First pass: scan each row for maximal `-` runs of length ≥ 2 → horizontal slots; scan each column the same way → vertical slots. Store each slot as its list of cells.
Backtrack over slots in order. For the current slot, try every unused word whose length matches; it fits if each cell is `-` or already equals the word's letter at that position.
Place the word (saving each cell's prior char), mark it used, recurse to the next slot; on failure restore the saved chars and unmark. Return the grid when all slots are filled.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Enumerating slots is one O(R·C) pass. The search assigns words to S slots; in the worst case it tries permutations of the W words, each fit/place/undo costing O(L) for slot length L → O(W! · L). Space is the slots (O(S·L)) plus recursion depth O(S).
approaches.explanation:
Split the work into 'find the empty slots' and 'fill them'.

**Enumerate slots once.** Walk each row left to right; whenever you see a `-`, extend to the end of the run, and if that run has length ≥ 2 record the list of its cells as a horizontal slot. Do the same down each column for vertical slots. Now every legal word position is captured exactly once — no boundary re-checking during the search.

**Backtrack slot by slot.** Process `slots[i]`. For each word not yet used whose length equals the slot length, test the **fit**: for every cell in the slot, the grid must hold `-` (free) or the *same* letter the word would place (a crossing already filled by an earlier word). If it fits, write the word's letters into the slot — but first **save each cell's previous character** into a backup, because some of those cells may already belong to a crossing word. Mark the word used and recurse to `slots[i+1]`. If the recursion fails, restore the saved characters and unmark, then try the next word.

**Why the backup is the whole game.** When two words cross, the second word to be placed must not disturb the shared letter, and if a branch later fails we must restore *exactly* what was there — which might be a letter from a crossing word, not a `-`. Blanket-resetting to `-` would silently delete an already-correct crossing. Saving and restoring per cell makes undo exact.

**Termination.** When `i == len(slots)` every slot holds a word and all crossings are consistent (each placement was checked), so the grid is the unique solution.
approaches.insight: Modeling the grid as slots converts a 2-D placement puzzle into a 1-D constraint-satisfaction problem: assign words to slots so overlaps agree. The only stateful subtlety is undo — save each cell's prior contents so a failed branch restores crossing letters instead of erasing them.

pitfalls: Resetting cells to `-` on undo instead of restoring the saved characters — wipes a crossing word.
Treating single blanks as slots — only runs of length ≥ 2 qualify.
Forgetting the 'cell already equals the letter' branch in the fit check — rejects valid crossings.

commonMistakes: Restoring backtracked cells to `-` instead of their previous contents, erasing crossing words.
Placing words at arbitrary offsets without boundary checks, so a word overruns a `+`.
Treating a single isolated blank as a slot instead of requiring a run of length ≥ 2.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Undo that erases crossings
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On backtrack the cells must be restored to exactly what they held before — which may be letters from a crossing word already placed. Blanket-resetting to `-` deletes that crossing and corrupts the grid.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for (r, c) in slot:
    grid[r][c] = '-'      # WRONG: wipes crossing letters too
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
backup = [grid[r][c] for (r, c) in slot]
# ... place, recurse ...
for j, (r, c) in enumerate(slot):
    grid[r][c] = backup[j]   # restore exact prior contents

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Fit check that ignores existing crossings
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A cell already filled by a crossing word is not blank, but it's still a valid placement if it equals this word's letter. Requiring every cell to be `-` rejects all crossings.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: fits = all(grid[r][c] == '-' for (r, c) in slot)   # rejects valid crossings
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
fits = all(grid[r][c] == '-' or grid[r][c] == w[j]
           for j, (r, c) in enumerate(slot))

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing boundary check in brute placement
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without verifying the cell before the start and after the end are `+`/edge, a word can begin mid-run or overrun a wall, filling a non-slot.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// only checks bounds and matching letters
if (c + len <= 10 && lettersMatch) place();
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (c + len <= 10
    && (c == 0 || g[r][c-1] == '+')
    && (c + len == 10 || g[r][c+len] == '+')
    && lettersMatch) place();

patternNote: Constraint-satisfaction backtracking on a grid. Model the empty cells as slots, then assign words to slots with choose → check overlaps → recurse → undo. The defining detail is exact undo (save each cell's prior contents) so crossings survive a failed branch. The same shape powers Sudoku solvers and Word Search.
